lead: A beam bends cleanly only when the load line passes through one special point of its cross-section. That point is the shear centre, also called the flexural centre. Load there and the section bends without twisting. Load anywhere else, even through the centroid, and the section twists as it bends. Thin-walled channels, angles and Z-sections are common in purlins and crane rails, and their shear centre is usually not the centroid. This chapter finds the shear centre of a channel using shear flow.
prereq: You need: 4.1 for centroid and second moment of area, and 4.5 for shear flow q = VQ/I.

sections.h3: The point that gives pure bending

blocks.text: A transverse load on a beam produces a shear force V and a bending moment. The bending part is covered by the bending equation. The shear part is carried by shear stresses spread across the section. The resultant of those shear stresses acts along one line. Where that line cuts the cross-section is the shear centre.

If a load acts through the shear centre, the beam bends without twisting. If the load line misses it, the internal shear forces form a torque about the longitudinal axis, and the beam twists as well as bends. Twisting adds warping and extra shear stress, and can buckle a thin flange.

For a section with one axis of symmetry, the shear centre lies on that axis. For a doubly symmetric section such as a rectangle, a circle or an I-section, it lies at the centroid. For a channel, an angle or a Z-section, it lies somewhere else. A channel is the standard example: its centroid lies between the web and the flange tips, on the flange side, while its shear centre lies outside the section, on the other side of the web.

Take a thin-walled channel with the web vertical and both flanges pointing to the right. A vertical shear force V acts on the section. In any wall, the shear flow q is the shear force per unit length along the wall, in N/m. It is found from q = VQ/I. Here Q is the first moment of area of the part of the section beyond the cut, about the neutral axis, in m³; I is the second moment of area of the whole section about the same axis, in m⁴.

In each flange, the shear flow runs horizontally. The flow in the top flange and the flow in the bottom flange run in opposite directions. These two horizontal forces are separated by the web depth h, so together they form a couple about the longitudinal axis. That couple is a torque. The vertical shear V acting through the web centreline does not cancel it. The section therefore twists.

Move the load line sideways by a distance e. The vertical force V now produces a balancing torque V e. No twist occurs when V e equals the flange couple. Solving that balance gives the shear centre offset for a thin-walled channel with equal flanges and uniform wall thickness t:

blocks.where: e is the distance from the web centreline to the shear centre, measured on the side away from the flanges; b is the flange width from the web centreline to the free edge; h is the web depth between flange centrelines. Use the same length unit for b, h and e. The wall thickness t cancels out.

blocks.text: Use the formula only for a thin-walled channel with equal flanges. An I-section needs no offset because its flanges produce equal and opposite torques that cancel. A box section behaves in the same way.

A roof purlin of channel section is often loaded through its top flange, where the roof sheet sits. That load line is far from the shear centre, so the purlin tends to twist. Over time the twist can crack the sheet or fail the purlin. Designers either load through the shear centre, restrain the flanges, or choose a box or I-section.
The shear centre is a property of the section geometry. It does not depend on the size of the load or on the material. Find it once and you know where to apply transverse loads to avoid torsion.

Only a few syllabi go beyond the channel formula. Full unsymmetrical bending needs the shear flow around the whole wall and the principal axes; that is advanced study. For beam design against bending and shear stress, see 4.7.

figure.caption: An off-centre load twists the channel; shear flow in the two flanges creates a torque. A load at the shear centre, 37.5 mm from the web centreline, balances that torque and the section bends without twisting.

spec.title: Shear centre idea
spec.aria: Flowchart: an off-centre load twists the section; shear flow in the flanges creates a balancing torque at an offset e, so a load through the shear centre causes no twist.

examples.question: A thin-walled steel channel has web depth h = 200 mm measured between flange centrelines, equal flange width b = 100 mm measured from the web centreline to the free edge, and uniform thickness t = 3 mm. Locate the shear centre. State on which side of the web it lies.
steps: List the data: b = 100 mm, h = 200 mm, t = 3 mm. The section is a thin-walled channel with equal flanges, so the formula applies.
Compute the numerator: b² = (100 mm)² = 10 000 mm².
The shear centre lies on the horizontal axis of symmetry. The flanges point one way, so e is measured on the opposite side of the web centreline, outside the web.
Check the thickness: t appears in Q and in I, so it cancels. Changing t does not move the shear centre.
examples.answer: The shear centre is 37.5 mm from the web centreline, on the side away from the flanges (outside the web).

traps: The centroid is not the shear centre for a channel. The centroid lies between the web and the flange tips (about 25 mm from the web centreline in the example), while the shear centre lies outside the section on the other side of the web, 37.5 mm from the web centreline. A load through the centroid still twists the channel.
Measure b from the web centreline to the flange tip. Using the full flange width twice, or measuring from the flange edge, gives a wrong e.
Measure h between flange centrelines. Using the overall depth including flange thickness shifts e slightly; the formula assumes thin walls.
The offset is on the side away from the flanges. Drawing e inside the channel reverses the balancing torque.
The formula is for equal flanges and uniform thickness. Do not apply it to a lipped channel, an unequal-flange channel or a thick-walled section without a proper shear flow analysis.

quiz.a: The shear centre is the point in a cross-section through which a transverse load must act to produce bending without twisting.

quiz.q: Where is the shear centre of a doubly symmetric I-section?
quiz.a: At the centroid, because the shear flow is symmetric and produces no torque about the centroid.

quiz.q: Why does a vertical load through the centroid of a channel twist the section?
quiz.a: The horizontal shear flows in the two flanges are opposite and form a couple about the longitudinal axis. The centroid is not on the line of the resultant shear force, so that couple is not balanced by the load.

quiz.q: A thin-walled channel has b = 80 mm and h = 150 mm. Find e.
quiz.a: e = b²/(2b + h/3) = 6400/(160 + 50) = 6400/210 = 30.5 mm from the web centreline, away from the flanges.

quiz.q: For the same channel, b is doubled to 160 mm while h stays 150 mm. Find the new e.
quiz.a: e = 160²/(2×160 + 150/3) = 25 600/(320 + 50) = 25 600/370 = 69.2 mm from the web centreline, away from the flanges.

quiz.q: A roof purlin of channel section is loaded through its top flange. Explain what happens and give one remedy.
quiz.a: The load line is far from the shear centre, so the purlin twists as well as bends. The twist adds warping and shear stress and can buckle the flange. Remedy: use a restrained or box section, or apply the load through the shear centre with a suitable bracket.

quiz.q: Why does the wall thickness t not appear in the channel formula?
quiz.a: The first moment of area Q used in q = VQ/I and the second moment of area I are both proportional to t. So t cancels in Q/I: the shear flow, the flange force and hence e do not contain t.

quiz.q: Compare an I-section and a channel of similar depth for a load applied at the web. Which twists and why?
quiz.a: The I-section is doubly symmetric. Its shear centre is at the centroid, on the web, so a load through the web centreline does not twist it. The channel has its shear centre outside the web, so the same load line misses the shear centre and the channel twists.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cold-formed steel design codes treat shear centre and torsional warping together, because thin open sections twist easily. Aircraft spars and crane rails use the same idea. Search for 'shear centre of thin-walled open sections', 'warping constant' and 'Vlasov torsion' to go further.
